prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and active peptide forms of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six openings placed GLP-1 first, and I agree on the merits rather than because of that unanimity. The chain from proglucagon processing, to the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, to its insulinotropic, satiety and gastric actions, to receptor-based drugs is original, mechanistically clear and independently confirmed in large outcome trials. It is also a physiology-to-medicine story of the kind this prize was built to recognise, and its effects now extend beyond glycaemia to cardiovascular and renal outcomes. A prize framed around the discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form is cleaner than one framed around any single drug, and it is also defensible against the demand that a Nobel reward discovery rather than product development.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. The identification of the active peptide form is contested between Mojsov and others, notably Habener, who is not among the credited names. Any three-person cut also leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue design is what put the biology into patients. A prize that rewards only the physiology could be seen as overlooking the step that made the medicine, and a prize that includes industrial drug design risks diluting the discovery claim. I cannot fully resolve either problem from the supplied credit list.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks GLP-1 first but names Knudsen in place of Mojsov, because the Mojsov credit is contested in the literature and the long-acting analogue design is decisive for the clinical result.
responses.response: I take the concern about Mojsov's contested priority seriously and it is my main reservation. I still keep her over Knudsen. The Nobel tradition in this field rewards the discovery of the mechanism, and the identification of the active peptide is a discovery step that Drucker and Holst's physiology builds on. Knudsen's work is outstanding translational design, but it follows from that biology and could be recognised under a later, drug-focused framing. If the committee's own review of priority shows Mojsov's claim cannot be sustained, I would then prefer to substitute Knudsen rather than a different candidate. I would not make that substitution on the strength of public controversy alone.

responses.point: Linnarsson also ranks GLP-1 first, but stresses that the credit among peptide identification, physiology and drug engineering cannot be settled from the list, and he names Knudsen as a strong alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the allocation is unresolved, and I would rather say so than present the trio as obvious. Where I differ is on what the prize is for. If we reward the discovery of GLP-1 as an incretin and its physiology, the trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is coherent. If we reward the therapy, then Knudsen belongs and Mojsov's role becomes less central. We should decide the framing before debating the names, because the names follow from it. My view is that the first framing is the more defensible one.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks the unfolded protein response second as a conceptually clean ER-to-nucleus signalling discovery with a natural two-person pairing of Walter and Mori, and treats PERK and the integrated stress response as separable.
responses.response: I agree that Walter and Mori make the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and for that reason I keep B003 as my first alternative. My reservation is the one you raise yourself, that the integrated stress response and the PERK and ATF6 branches may be hard to separate from the core story, and that human therapeutic validation is thin. That makes the medical case weaker than for GLP-1, but it does not undermine the basic discovery. I would not combine B003 with B034, because a two-part prize would have to cut the GLP-1 credit to two names and that is a worse trade.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks optogenetics fifth and treats it as a high-impact methodological invention whose six-name credit list makes any three-person allocation contestable.
responses.response: From my own circuit work I agree that optogenetics changed how we test causality in neural circuits, and I ranked it second. I would not put it forward as the preferred prize, though. It is a tool rather than a discovery of disease mechanism, and I do not see a defensible three-person cut across Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg, Boyden, Miesenböck and Deisseroth. My field familiarity gives me no reason to rank it above candidates whose clinical effect is demonstrated, and I will not let it.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide form holds up on a closer review of the primary record, and whether Habener's omission from the credited names should change the configuration.
Whether the prize should be framed around hormone physiology or around the resulting drugs, which decides between Mojsov and Knudsen.
Whether any of the long-term safety questions for incretin therapy would change the maturity assessment.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented collaborations (Grillner, Ernfors, and a 2009 paper with Perlmann) concern motor, pain and stem-cell neuroscience and do not involve any shortlisted candidate.
